question: A study shows that patients with higher anxiety report higher pain levels. Why can the researcher NOT claim that anxiety causes the pain?

options.A: Because anxiety is an experimental variable
options.B: Because pain cannot be measured using numerical scales
options.C: Because the sample size was likely too small to matter
options.D: Because correlational designs do not test cause and effect

explanation: Spot on! Finding a connection between two things just shows they move together; it doesn't prove one actually caused the other. Correlation is not causation!

question: How can experiencing a severe illness during childhood affect a person later in life?

options.A: It ensures the individual becomes a proficient medical doctor
options.B: It completely eliminates any fear of normal aging processes
options.C: It can create a lasting hypersensitivity to bodily vulnerabilities
options.D: It guarantees immunity against developing anxiety disorders

explanation: Early life bumps and health scares can teach a child that the human body is super fragile, planting the seeds for health anxiety down the road.

question: What is the main public health goal of achieving high herd immunity within a community?

options.A: To guarantee lifelong immunity without booster doses
options.B: To protect vulnerable individuals who cannot receive vaccines
options.C: To reduce the financial cost of hospital admissions
options.D: To completely eliminate all known chronic illnesses

explanation: When most of the population is vaccinated, it creates a protective barrier that stops infectious agents from reaching people who are too young or sick to get vaccinated. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T61#GNS214_U1_T61_h1)

question: Who are considered key stakeholders in community mental health mobilisation?

options.A: Only patients currently admitted to psychiatric wards
options.B: Foreign investors and international tourists
options.C: Traditional leaders, religious heads, and local groups
options.D: Only certified psychiatric doctors from abroad

explanation: Local leaders and grassroots groups hold the trust of the community and are vital partners for successful health campaigns. [learn more](GNS314_U4_T7#GNS314_U4_T7_h3)

question: What is the main sign of a food fad?

options.A: It is a lifelong medical diet prescribed by a qualified physician.
options.B: It is a government-regulated nutrition program for school children.
options.C: It is a traditional cultural meal plan passed down for generations.
options.D: It is an intense and short-lived dietary trend without scientific backing.

explanation: Food fads come and go very quickly. They usually make big health claims that have zero real science behind them. You've got this!

question: What is the main reason we group and organize medical supplies in a ward?

options.A: To reduce the total number of items ordered each month
options.B: To prevent medication errors and speed up retrieval
options.C: To make the pharmacy department look neat and tidy
options.D: To ensure patients pay higher fees for their treatments

explanation: A well-organized ward helps you find what you need in a hurry. When every second counts, clear placement keeps your patients safe and cuts down on mistakes.

question: When planning meals for a pregnant patient in your community, what should guide you the most?

options.A: Focusing exclusively on raw vegetable diets
options.B: Using only expensive imported vitamin supplements
options.C: Eliminating all traditional family recipes
options.D: Local food availability and household finances

explanation: You nailed clinical reality! Advice is useless if the family can't afford it or find the ingredients nearby. Always keep it practical!

question: A community health nurse notices high rates of childhood stunting and anemia in an isolated village. What underlying distribution problem is most likely contributing to this?

options.A: An oversupply of refrigerated trucks delivering too many vegetables
options.B: Excessive availability of free nutritional supplements from clinics
options.C: Strict local laws that prohibit families from cooking traditional meals
options.D: Inability to consistently transport diverse, fresh foods to the area

explanation: Poor transport links starve remote populations of the varied nutrients required for healthy childhood development. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T025#GNS227_U2_T025_h7)

question: What communication tool helps nurses pass structured and concise patient or situation data during a crisis?

options.A: Casual text messages sent without checking details
options.B: SBAR (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation)
options.C: Complex medical research articles from foreign journals
options.D: Long narrative diary entries written at the end of the shift

explanation: SBAR gives healthcare workers a quick, organized way to share essential facts without wasting time during emergencies. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T2#GNS315_U5_T2_h6)

question: What is the very first step when starting up or running a DRF cycle?

options.A: Selling the expired drugs to local traders
options.B: Increasing the profit margin on all antibiotics
options.C: Writing off all debts owed by defaulting patients
options.D: Quantification and forecasting of drug needs

explanation: You got it! Before buying anything, you have to calculate how much medicine the hospital actually uses based on past patient attendance.

question: Why is a predictable daily routine important in a half-way house?

options.A: It promotes stability and reduces anxiety for residents
options.B: It replaces the need for any medication or therapy
options.C: It ensures that nurses have less paperwork to complete
options.D: It punishes residents who wake up late in the morning

explanation: Great thinking! Structure and predictability help individuals with mental health conditions feel secure, calm, and organized.

question: Imagine a BP machine reads 200/120 mmHg three times in a row for a healthy person whose real BP is 120/80 mmHg. How would you describe this tool?

options.A: Both high reliability and high validity
options.B: High reliability but low validity
options.C: Both low reliability and low validity
options.D: Low reliability and high validity

explanation: It gave the exact same wrong number repeatedly, so it's consistent (reliable), but completely off the mark (invalid). Classic case of high reliability, low validity!

question: A nurse accidentally gives the wrong dose because two different drugs have almost identical labels. In a Just Culture, how is this viewed?

options.A: Intentional harm requiring criminal investigation
options.B: Human error requiring system and package redesign
options.C: At-risk behavior requiring strict disciplinary suspension
options.D: Reckless behavior requiring immediate termination

explanation: Spot on! Confusing look-alike labels is an innocent human slip. Instead of blaming the nurse, a Just Culture fixes the faulty packaging so it doesn't happen again.

question: What is the main goal of the DASH diet for someone with high blood pressure?

options.A: To increase potassium, calcium, and fiber while reducing sodium
options.B: To replace all fluid intake with specialized herbal teas
options.C: To encourage rapid weight loss through strict calorie counting
options.D: To eliminate all carbohydrates from the daily meal plan

explanation: DASH focuses on whole foods packed with good minerals like potassium and calcium while cutting back on salt to protect the heart.

question: What are the three core parts of the epidemiological triad used to study diseases?

options.A: Infection, illness, and recovery
options.B: Agent, host, and environment
options.C: Vector, parasite, and human
options.D: Bacteria, virus, and protozoa

explanation: Spot on! The epidemiological triad looks at the interacting relationship between the agent, the host, and their environment to understand how diseases spread.

question: What is the main purpose of writing clinical notes in home health care?

options.A: To provide reading material for family members during the evening
options.B: To replace verbal handoff reports between incoming and outgoing shifts
options.C: To serve as a legal record and ensure continuity of care among team members
options.D: To prove to the patient that the nurse visited their home on schedule

explanation: Spot on! Good documentation keeps the whole healthcare team on the same page and serves as a reliable legal record of the care you provided. Keep up the good charting habits!

question: What is the main job of 'inclusion criteria' in a nursing research study?

options.A: To explain how data will be analyzed using statistical software
options.B: To define the specific traits a participant must have to join the study
options.C: To list the reasons why a patient should be given extra medication
options.D: To describe the equipment used to measure patient vital signs

explanation: You nailed it! Inclusion criteria are simply the 'welcome checklist' of traits a person must have to be part of your research.

question: Why is growing different types of crops (crop diversity) on small farms good for community nutrition?

options.A: It stops pests from destroying the main staple crop
options.B: It prevents seasonal vitamin deficiencies by providing varied nutrients
options.C: It completely eliminates the need for agricultural irrigation
options.D: It ensures that farmers only grow what sells for the highest profit

explanation: When farms grow a variety of crops, people get different vitamins and nutrients, which stops specific deficiency diseases. Brilliant concept to remember!

question: According to the WHO moments for hand hygiene, when is Moment 5?

options.A: Immediately before making physical contact with the patient
options.B: After accidentally touching spilled blood on the floor
options.C: After touching inanimate objects in the patient's immediate surroundings
options.D: Before performing a sterile dressing change

explanation: Moment 5 is all about cleaning your hands after touching things around the patient, like adjusting the bed rail or bedside table.

question: A ward has very sick patients and several junior nurses on duty. What is the best staffing approach?

options.A: Pair junior nurses with experienced senior nurses
options.B: Send all the junior nurses home to rest
options.C: Ignore the patient acuity levels when scheduling
options.D: Assign all critical patients to the most junior nurse

explanation: You got it! Teaming up junior nurses with experienced seniors keeps patients safe and helps the junior staff learn safely.

question: For weak, frail patients, why do we recommend small, frequent meals instead of three big ones?

options.A: They prevent the patient from feeling overwhelmed and reduce fatigue during eating.
options.B: They completely eliminate the need for any fiber in the diet.
options.C: They stop the stomach from producing normal digestive acids.
options.D: They guarantee that the patient will consume twice as many calories.

explanation: Eating a huge plate of food can exhaust a frail patient. Smaller, tasty portions throughout the day make eating feel manageable and less tiring.

question: Why does the body increase blood volume so massively during pregnancy?

options.A: To store extra calcium needed for the baby's developing bones
options.B: To increase the physical strength of the maternal heart muscle
options.C: To provide extra fluid protection against blood loss during delivery
options.D: To completely prevent the mother from ever catching infections

explanation: Nature is amazing! The extra blood acts as a safety cushion for the blood loss that naturally happens when giving birth. Brilliant design, right?

question: Which of the following belongs to the epidemiological component of a health profile?

options.A: Prevalence of malaria and malnutrition rates
options.B: Total number of children enrolled in primary school
options.C: Condition of roads leading to the primary health center
options.D: Average monthly income of market women

explanation: Epidemiology looks at disease patterns, illness rates, and health conditions affecting the population. [learn more](GNS124_U3_T6#GNS124_U3_T6_h3)

question: Why must a nurse monitor the heart and lungs closely when a patient has severe kidney failure?

options.A: The kidneys directly control the electrical rhythm of the heart muscle.
options.B: Medications given for kidney failure only work if the lungs are healthy.
options.C: Failure in one organ system quickly triggers problems in interdependent systems.
options.D: Kidneys are located right next to the heart and lungs in the body cavity.

explanation: You're thinking like a real nurse! Kidneys handle fluids and electrolytes; when they stop working, fluid backs up into the lungs and affects heart function.

question: A patient has an autoimmune condition where their insulin-making cells are destroyed. What lab finding is most likely?

options.A: Dangerously low blood sugar caused by excess hormone release
options.B: Rapid weight gain due to slowed metabolic breakdown
options.C: Elevated blood glucose levels due to a lack of insulin
options.D: Increased water retention and high blood pressure

explanation: Without insulin (hyposecretion), glucose can't easily enter the body's cells to be used for energy. Instead, it builds up in the bloodstream, leading to high blood sugar.

question: Which ethical rule reminds nurses to make sure their actions cause no extra harm to a vulnerable patient?

options.A: Non-maleficence
options.B: Veracity
options.C: Autonomy
options.D: Justice

explanation: Non-maleficence simply means 'do no harm'. As nurses, protecting our patients from extra injury or distress is our core duty.

question: What is a common misconception about herbal and complementary medications?

options.A: They can only be bought with a doctor's prescription
options.B: They are chemically identical to synthetic antibiotics
options.C: They never interact with standard hospital drugs
options.D: They are completely harmless because they are natural

explanation: Patients often think natural means safe, but herbs contain active chemicals that can cause serious side effects or drug interactions. [learn more](GNS125_U2_T1#GNS125_U2_T1_h5)

question: Which of these hospital items is considered critical and needs full sterilization?

options.A: A surgical scalpel blade
options.B: A reusable blood pressure cuff
options.C: A stethoscope chest piece
options.D: A bedside plastic commode

explanation: Brilliant! Scalpels cut deep into sterile body tissues, so they must be 100% free of all germs and spores through proper sterilization.

question: What is the main difference between direct medical costs and direct non-medical costs?

options.A: Medical costs involve clinical treatment, while non-medical costs involve support services like transport
options.B: Medical costs are optional, while non-medical costs are mandatory for survival
options.C: Medical costs occur in the hospital, while non-medical costs occur at home
options.D: Medical costs are paid by the government, while non-medical costs are paid in cash

explanation: Direct medical costs pay for actual clinical care, while direct non-medical costs cover practical expenses like getting to and from the hospital.

question: An older adult patient with orthostatic hypotension is preparing for discharge. What instruction should the nurse include in their care plan?

options.A: Avoid wearing compression socks because they block blood flow.
options.B: Drink less fluid during the day to avoid frequent bathroom trips.
options.C: Stand up as quickly as possible to get blood moving.
options.D: Sit on the edge of the bed for a minute before standing up.

explanation: Sitting on the edge of the bed allows the cardiovascular system to adjust to posture changes, preventing orthostatic dizziness. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T16#GNS123_U3_T16_h7)

question: What does health equity mean?

options.A: Doctors and nurses earn the same monthly salary
options.B: Every hospital receives the exact same amount of money
options.C: All patients pay identical fees for prescriptions
options.D: Everyone gets resources based on their specific needs

explanation: Equity focuses on fairness and giving extra support to disadvantaged groups to achieve equal health outcomes. [learn more](GST321_U6_T3#GST321_U6_T3_h5)

question: Which action should a nurse take when conducting a mental health screening in a community clinic?

options.A: Build trusting rapport and explain the purpose of the screening questions
options.B: Diagnosing the patient with a psychiatric disorder immediately on the spot
options.C: Rushing through the questions so the patient does not feel uncomfortable
options.D: Ignoring non-verbal cues and focusing strictly on the written score

explanation: Establishing trust and explaining the purpose of screening helps reduce anxiety and encourages honest answers from the patient. [learn more](GNS314_U5_T1#GNS314_U5_T1_h6)

question: What is the main job of foetal circulation?

options.A: To supply oxygen and nutrients from the mother
options.B: To pump blood directly into the mother's kidneys
options.C: To circulate air through the baby's developing lungs
options.D: To filter all waste through the baby's own kidneys

explanation: You've got this! Since a baby in the womb cannot breathe air or eat food yet, the placenta steps in to bring oxygen and nutrients straight from the mother's blood. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T006#GNS226_U2_T006_h1)

question: Why do bacterial toxins in the gut cause diarrhea?

options.A: They block the reabsorption of solid waste in the rectum
options.B: They stimulate excess fluid secretion into the bowel lumen
options.C: They cause permanent paralysis of the abdominal muscles
options.D: They completely stop the production of digestive enzymes

explanation: When toxins irritate your gut lining, it reacts by rushing a lot of water and salt out into your intestines, causing watery stool to flush the germs out.

question: Why do teenagers sometimes take big risks or act on impulse?

options.A: Brain development is completely finished by age ten
options.B: Parents encourage dangerous activities to build character
options.C: Teens explore identity and independence while their decision-making brain regions mature
options.D: Risky behaviors are mandatory symptoms of hormonal disease

explanation: The brain's impulse-control center is still under construction during these years, which explains why teens love quick thrills and trying new things.

question: Which body regulates and licenses nursing practice in Nigeria?

options.A: The West African Health Community Bureau
options.B: The Federal Ministry of Information Technology
options.C: The Nigerian Medical Association Board
options.D: The Nursing and Midwifery Council of Nigeria

explanation: Great job! The NMCN is our guiding body. They set the rules, handle licensing, and make sure nursing standards are kept high across Nigeria.

question: What is an important nursing check after a patient has an upper GI scope (endoscopy)?

options.A: Giving strong oral laxatives to clear out remaining dye
options.B: Putting warm compresses on the tummy every 15 minutes
options.C: Checking that the patient's gag reflex is back before giving food or water
options.D: Pushing the patient to eat a heavy meal right away to get their strength back

explanation: The throat spray numbs the back of the throat during the scope. If you feed them before the gag reflex returns, they could easily choke or aspirate.

question: Which of these is a major home hazard that can cause older adults to fall?

options.A: Having too many windows in the bedroom
options.B: Loose carpets and inadequate lighting
options.C: Using electric fans during warm weather
options.D: Brightly painted walls in the hallway

explanation: Simple things like dim hallways or loose rugs are major tripping hazards. Home safety assessments are a key part of community nursing care for the elderly!

question: What substance must team up with vitamin B12 in the stomach so it can be absorbed properly in the lower small intestine?

options.A: Hydrochloric acid
options.B: Pancreatic lipase
options.C: Intrinsic factor
options.D: Bile salts

explanation: You got it! Stomach parietal cells secrete intrinsic factor, which binds to B12 like a VIP pass so the terminal ileum can safely absorb it.

question: What makes professional malpractice different from general negligence?

options.A: Malpractice can only be tried in criminal court rather than civil court
options.B: Malpractice requires specialized professional training and a breach of standards
options.C: Negligence only applies to doctors while malpractice applies to nurses
options.D: Negligence requires the patient to suffer permanent physical disability

explanation: Malpractice is basically negligence, but specifically by someone with professional training (like a nurse or doctor) who breaks the standard of care.

question: Why do inactivated (killed) vaccines usually need booster doses compared to live vaccines?

options.A: They do not multiply in the body, so they trigger a weaker immune response.
options.B: They contain toxic chemicals that destroy early antibody production.
options.C: They target multiple diseases simultaneously instead of a single pathogen.
options.D: They dissolve too quickly inside the muscular tissue before antibodies form.

explanation: Makes total sense, right? Since dead germs cannot multiply inside you, your body often needs a few extra reminders (boosters) to build long-term protection.

question: Which of these is a great example of intrinsic motivation?

options.A: Avoiding a written warning from the director of nursing
options.B: Receiving a monthly cash bonus for perfect attendance
options.C: Finding personal joy and satisfaction in helping a patient recover
options.D: Competing with colleagues for the nurse of the month plaque

explanation: Intrinsic motivation comes from within—like the warm feeling you get when your patient smiles and gets better. No award needed!

question: When a nursing manager has to settle a dispute between two departments, what should be their main goal?

options.A: Collaborative problem-solving and patient safety
options.B: Ignoring the issue until it resolves on its own
options.C: Punishing the staff members who started the argument
options.D: Closing one of the departments involved

explanation: Spot on! Good leaders look for the root cause and solve problems together, always keeping patient safety at the heart of it all.

question: A patient has a stubborn, hard mass of stool that normal enemas can't shift. What procedure is best here?

options.A: A rectal washout
options.B: An intravenous fluid bolus
options.C: A nasogastric tube insertion
options.D: An oral laxative challenge

explanation: When standard enemas aren't strong enough to break up severe blockages, a rectal washout provides the extra mechanical help needed.

question: In a risk pool, what happens to the money paid by members who stay completely healthy?

options.A: Their unused contributions help pay for the medical care of sick members
options.B: The insurance scheme is forced to shut down immediately
options.C: Their money is refunded in cash at the end of every month
options.D: They are penalized with higher premium rates next year

explanation: Great job! Risk pooling works because the contributions of healthy members cover the costs of those who fall ill, balancing everything out.

question: What do geographical boundaries (like rivers or roads) give to a traditional community?

options.A: Clear physical limits and a defined space for service delivery
options.B: Guaranteed financial funding from international agencies
options.C: Absolute immunity from infectious disease outbreaks
options.D: Complete isolation from neighboring populations

explanation: Physical borders make it easy for nurses to map out an area and plan where to bring healthcare services.

question: Which category of substances acts by slowing down brain activity and central nervous system functions?

options.A: Stimulants
options.B: Hallucinogens
options.C: Inhalants
options.D: Depressants

explanation: Correct! Depressants like alcohol put the brakes on the nervous system, which can dangerously lower breathing and heart rates if taken in excess.

question: Which of these is a key feature of teacher-centred teaching methods?

options.A: The classroom has no formal structure or predefined schedule
options.B: The teacher observes quietly while students teach each other
options.C: The students spend all class time performing independent research
options.D: The educator acts as the primary information giver while learners listen

explanation: In a teacher-centred setup (like a classic lecture), the instructor does most of the talking and passes information directly to the listening students.

question: In a fraction, what does the bottom number (the denominator) stand for?

options.A: The total number of equal parts making up the whole
options.B: The maximum adult dose limit
options.C: A metric conversion factor
options.D: The part ordered by the doctor

explanation: Think of a pizza! The denominator at the bottom tells you the total number of slices the whole pizza is cut into.

question: What can happen if you use a sensitive smart bed alarm on a patient who is fully independent and active?

options.A: Immediate mechanical failure of the bed's lifting actuators
options.B: Unnecessary anxiety for the patient and alarm fatigue for nurses
options.C: Automatic cancellation of physician medication orders
options.D: Rapid depletion of the bed's internal backup battery

explanation: If a bed keeps beeping every time an active patient moves, it stresses the patient out and trains staff to ignore the noise—which is called alarm fatigue!

question: Which of the following is NOT a common challenge faced by community midwives in rural Nigeria?

options.A: Insecure terrain and difficult geographical transportation routes
options.B: Irregular salary payments and financial delay issues
options.C: Professional isolation due to working alone in remote outposts
options.D: Immediate access to fully equipped advanced intensive care units

explanation: Rural community midwives lack access to advanced intensive care units; their reality is marked by resource limitations and isolation, not surplus equipment. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T14#GNS225_U3_T14_h8)

question: A new mother on the ward is bleeding heavily two hours after delivery, and her uterus feels soft and boggy. What is the likely cause?

options.A: Eclamptic seizure
options.B: Obstructed labor
options.C: Pelvic inflammatory disease
options.D: Uterine atony

explanation: When the uterus fails to contract firmly (atony), the blood vessels stay open and bleeding happens. A firm massage and oxytocics are usually our best friends here!

question: Why do babies of young mothers often face more malnutrition and infections as they grow?

options.A: Breast milk produced by teenagers is naturally toxic to infants
options.B: Cultural laws forbid young mothers from feeding their babies solid foods
options.C: Infants born to young mothers have stronger immune systems that reject food
options.D: The young mother often lacks the knowledge, resources, and autonomy for proper childcare

explanation: Correct! Inexperience and a lack of support make it hard for young mums to provide the best care and nutrition.

question: Which of these is a mineral-based drug commonly used to neutralize stomach acid?

options.A: Penicillin G
options.B: Morphine sulfate
options.C: Digoxin extract
options.D: Calcium carbonate

explanation: Calcium carbonate is a mineral compound often found in over-the-counter antacids to quickly soothe heartburn.

question: Which of these is NOT a common cause of high potassium (hyperkalemia)?

options.A: Taking medications that hold onto potassium
options.B: Using a diuretic that causes potassium loss
options.C: Advanced chronic kidney disease
options.D: Breakdown of damaged muscle tissue

explanation: You nailed it! Potassium-wasting diuretics actually flush potassium out of the body, so they cause low potassium (hypokalemia) instead.

question: Why is a 16-year-old girl biologically more vulnerable to catching an STI during intercourse?

options.A: Rapid regeneration of damaged epithelial tissue
options.B: Excessive production of thick, protective mucus lining
options.C: Complete absence of white blood cells in the vaginal canal
options.D: Cervical ectopy with a larger area of vulnerable cells

explanation: You got it! Teenage reproductive tracts have cervical ectopy, exposing delicate cells that make it easier for germs to enter.

question: Why must you take off your gloves before removing your isolation gown during doffing?

options.A: To make it easier to tie the gown strings behind your back for the next shift
options.B: To prevent contaminating your hands and clothing with germs on the outside of the gown
options.C: To ensure the gown remains sterile for the next healthcare worker
options.D: To save time while exiting the patient care area in a busy ward

explanation: You're doing great! Your gloves carry the most germs, so taking them off first stops you from accidentally spreading pathogens to your clean hands and uniform.

question: What is the truest way to know if a continuing education training program was actually successful?

options.A: Checking how many participants filled out the seminar evaluation form
options.B: Verifying that all attendees stayed awake throughout the presentation
options.C: Observing if nurses apply what they learned to improve patient bedside care
options.D: Counting how many hours the lecture room lights remained switched on

explanation: Paper evaluations are nice, but real success shows up at the bedside when patients receive better, safer care because of what you learned!

question: Why does the body rely on both innate and adaptive defenses?

options.A: Innate destroys viruses while adaptive only handles bacterial infections
options.B: Innate immunity creates antibodies while adaptive creates physical barriers
options.C: Adaptive defense works entirely independently of the innate system
options.D: Innate provides immediate defense while adaptive targets specific invaders later

explanation: Spot on! Innate immunity jumps in instantly to buy time, while the adaptive system gears up to launch a precise, targeted attack.

question: What two measurements are used to calculate cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP) in the brain?

options.A: Mean arterial pressure and intracranial pressure
options.B: Systolic blood pressure and respiratory rate
options.C: Heart rate and central venous pressure
options.D: Oxygen saturation and core body temperature

explanation: You find the CPP by taking the mean arterial pressure and subtracting the intracranial pressure. You've got this formula down!

question: When you are cleaning a wound, what is the safest direction to wipe?

options.A: From the outer edges inward to the center
options.B: From the cleanest area to the dirtiest area
options.C: In a wild circular motion all over the skin
options.D: From the bottom of the wound straight up

explanation: Always move from clean to dirty! This golden rule stops you from dragging germs from the surrounding skin right back into the open wound.

question: Why does the infection control team monitor how well hospital surfaces are cleaned?

options.A: To make sure the hospital floors always shine brightly for visiting inspectors
options.B: Because many harmful pathogens can survive on dry hospital surfaces for long periods
options.C: To keep the housekeeping department busy between their regular meal breaks
options.D: Because cleaning chemicals are expensive and must be rationed carefully

explanation: Correct! Germs can hide out on bedrails, trays, and tables for ages if we don't clean them properly.

question: Why should the vertical axis on a bar chart usually start at zero?

options.A: To make all the bars look exactly the same height
options.B: To hide negative values from the reader
options.C: To prevent exaggerating small differences between groups
options.D: To ensure the chart fits onto a standard notebook page

explanation: Starting at zero maintains correct visual proportions so readers do not misinterpret minor changes as massive clinical differences. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T4#GNS224_U2_T4_h4)

question: What should a nurse do immediately if they spot a break in sterile technique?

options.A: Report the contamination and replace the compromised item immediately
options.B: Ignore it if nobody else saw it happen
options.C: Wipe the contaminated instrument with an alcohol swab and keep using it
options.D: Wait until the surgery is completely finished before mentioning it

explanation: Spot on! Patient safety comes first always. Never sweep a contamination under the rug—speak up and swap it out right away.

question: Which of the following is linked as an environmental trigger for developing MS?

options.A: Living close to sea level in tropical zones
options.B: Engaging in heavy physical labor outdoors
options.C: Eating a diet high in processed carbohydrates
options.D: Past viral infections like Epstein-Barr virus

explanation: While the exact cause isn't fully pinned down, certain past viral infections are believed to help trigger this abnormal immune response in vulnerable people.

question: What is the fastest and preferred energy source for your brain and nerves?

options.A: Glucose from carbohydrates
options.B: Fatty acids from dietary lipids
options.C: Amino acids from proteins
options.D: Vitamins from fresh fruit

explanation: Think of carbohydrates as premium fuel! They quickly break down into glucose, which is the brain's absolute favorite energy source.

question: Which of these is a biophysiological measure?

options.A: Interview transcript text
options.B: Open-ended survey response
options.C: Blood glucose level
options.D: Patient satisfaction score

explanation: Biophysiological measures are physical or chemical checks on the body, like checking blood sugar or temperature.

question: What do we call the tiny hair-like structures inside the ear that bend to trigger nerve signals?

options.A: Tympanic fibers
options.B: Cerumen
options.C: Ossicles
options.D: Stereocilia

explanation: Stereocilia sit proudly on top of hair cells. When inner ear fluid moves, these little hairs bend and kick off electrical signals to the brain.

question: What is a major reason people in Nigeria often delay going to modern hospitals?

options.A: An excess of free hospitals in every rural village
options.B: Mandatory international health insurance for all citizens
options.C: The complete absence of any traditional healing practices
options.D: Financial constraints and out-of-pocket health spending

explanation: True. Having to pay out-of-pocket without easy health insurance often makes folks wait until an illness gets really bad before seeking care.

question: Which of these is NOT a helpful community health strategy for managing sickle cell anaemia?

options.A: Educating the public to dispel myths about spiritual causes
options.B: Encouraging families to hide children with symptoms from public view
options.C: Providing accessible pre-marital genotype screening clinics
options.D: Training primary healthcare nurses to offer basic genetic counseling

explanation: Stigma is harmful! Hiding children only delays vital medical care and isolates them. Community health nursing is all about education, openness, and support.

question: What is a bone fracture?

options.A: A stretching injury to skeletal muscle fibers
options.B: A severe infection inside the bone marrow
options.C: A complete tearing of a ligament near a joint
options.D: A break or disruption in the continuity of a bone

explanation: Simple and clear! A fracture just means the bone's structure has cracked or broken. You've got this!

question: What is the role of the fimbriae at the end of the fallopian tubes?

options.A: Catch the released egg from the ovary
options.B: Produce estrogen and progesterone
options.C: Secrete mucus to block foreign bacteria
options.D: Anchor the uterus to the pelvic wall

explanation: Fimbriae are fringe-like fingers that wave over the ovary at ovulation to sweep the egg inside the fallopian tube. [learn more](GNS216_U2_T1#GNS216_U2_T1_h5)

question: What is the primary goal of discipline in nursing management?

options.A: To reduce the number of staff on duty
options.B: To correct behavior and protect patients
options.C: To enforce strict administrative control
options.D: To punish nurses who make mistakes

explanation: Management discipline aims to guide staff toward safe practices rather than simply punish them. [learn more](GST321_U1_T22#GST321_U1_T22_h1)

question: A doctor orders 250 mg of a suspension. The bottle label says 125 mg per 5 mL. How much should you measure?

options.B: 10 mL
options.C: 5 mL
options.D: 2.5 mL

explanation: Nice calculation! Dose ordered (250) divided by stock dose (125) equals 2. Multiply that by 5 mL, and you get 10 mL. You're getting the hang of this!

question: What is the primary purpose of clamping and occluding instruments?

options.A: To compress blood vessels and stop bleeding
options.B: To hold wound edges open for better visibility
options.C: To cut through tough bone and cartilage
options.D: To stitch the skin closed at the end of surgery

explanation: Clamping tools like hemostats squeeze bleeding vessels shut to maintain a clear field of vision during the procedure. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T9#GNS123_U5_T9_h2)

question: What exactly is salpingitis?

options.A: Bacterial colonization of the outer vulva
options.B: Malignant growth inside the uterine muscle wall
options.C: Fungal overgrowth within the vaginal vault
options.D: Infection and inflammation of the fallopian tubes

explanation: Salpingitis simply means inflammation in the fallopian tubes, usually caused by bacteria moving up from the lower reproductive tract. You've got this!

question: In a busy clinic with limited resources, what is one of the best ways to reduce airborne germ spread?

options.A: Turning off ceiling fans to stop particle circulation
options.B: Installing expensive high-efficiency particulate air scrubbers
options.C: Sealing all clinical rooms to prevent outside air entry
options.D: Ensuring optimal natural ventilation by opening windows and doors

explanation: Simple and effective! When high-tech ventilation isn't available, opening up doors and windows lets fresh outdoor air sweep those germs away.

question: What key visual finding does a clinician look for on the cervix during a speculum exam for acute cervicitis?

options.A: Pus-like discharge and tissue that bleeds easily
options.B: Complete closure of the internal cervical opening
options.C: Large fluid-filled cysts across the surface
options.D: Pale, dry, and glistening epithelial layers

explanation: During an exam, an angry, infected cervix often shows pus draining out and tissue that is fragile and bleeds at a touch.

question: Why is building a trusting relationship important during continuing care?

options.A: It legally binds the patient to live at the clinic
options.B: It keeps the patient engaged and compliant with their treatment plan
options.C: it stops family members from getting involved in care
options.D: It allows the nurse to avoid documenting patient interactions

explanation: Trust makes patients feel safe sharing their true feelings and concerns, which helps prevent them from dropping out of care. [learn more](GNS314_U4_T5#GNS314_U4_T5_h3)

question: A nurse wants to teach malaria prevention in a rural village with low literacy. What is the best design choice?

options.A: Include complex medical tables showing blood parasite counts over time.
options.B: Publish the guidelines exclusively in standard official government English.
options.C: Use clear local dialect translations paired with dominant, self-explanatory pictures.
options.D: Write long paragraphs explaining the exact life cycle of the female Anopheles mosquito.

explanation: Pictures combined with simple local language are a nurse's best friend for breaking through literacy and language barriers!

question: What does a 'trend' rule violation look like on a run chart?

options.A: Three points swinging wildly up and down every day
options.B: Six or more points landing directly on the median line
options.C: Five or more consecutive points steadily increasing or decreasing
options.D: Ten points scattered randomly across the upper half

explanation: A trend occurs when five or more consecutive data points move consistently in a single direction. [learn more](GST319_U1_T3#GST319_U1_T3_h5)

question: Why must a nurse carefully check blood compatibility before starting a blood transfusion?

options.A: To prevent the recipient's antibodies from attacking donor red blood cell antigens
options.B: To ensure the donor red blood cells do not dissolve in normal saline
options.C: To confirm the blood product contains enough white blood cells
options.D: To speed up the absorption of oxygen into the patient's bloodstream

explanation: Checking blood groups prevents mismatched antigens from triggering a dangerous attack by the patient's own antibodies.

question: When checking if an unresponsive patient is breathing normally, what is the maximum time a nurse should spend on this?

options.A: One minute
options.B: Thirty seconds
options.C: Ten seconds
options.D: Two minutes

explanation: Nice and quick! We check for breathing and a pulse at the same time, but we never want to waste precious seconds—keep it under 10 seconds so compressions aren't delayed.

question: How often must the injectable contraceptive NET-EN be given to keep working?

options.A: Every 16 weeks
options.B: Every 12 weeks
options.C: Every 24 weeks
options.D: Every 8 weeks

explanation: NET-EN uses a different progestin type that needs to be repeated every 2 months, which is 8 weeks.

question: Which drug is given immediately for a patient experiencing severe anaphylactic shock?

options.A: Furosemide
options.B: Paracetamol
options.C: Epinephrine
options.D: Insulin

explanation: Epinephrine given in the muscle acts fast to open up airways and reverse dangerous swelling and drops in blood pressure.

question: Why are lipids considered such an efficient energy source for resting tissues?

options.A: They convert instantly into glucose without needing any oxygen
options.B: They dissolve easily in water and travel quickly through the bloodstream
options.C: They bypass the liver entirely and go straight to the brain
options.D: They are energy-dense and yield high amounts of ATP through beta-oxidation

explanation: You got it! Fats pack a huge punch of energy in a small space, releasing tons of ATP when broken down through beta-oxidation.

question: A busy nurse decides to scan a patient's barcode taped to the computer instead of walking to the bedside to scan the wristband. What is this an example of?

options.A: Standard hospital protocol for rushed shifts
options.B: A dangerous clinical workaround
options.C: Proper use of bedside mobile technology
options.D: An efficient time-saving strategy

explanation: You got it! Scanning away from the bedside defeats the whole point of identity checks and opens the door to a wrong-patient medication error.

question: Which taste cells act like stem cells to replace older receptor cells?

options.A: Type IV cells
options.B: Type I cells
options.C: Type III cells
options.D: Type II cells

explanation: Type IV basal cells keep dividing to make brand-new taste receptor cells, since our taste cells wear out and replace themselves often.

question: What type of institution served as the primary sanctuary for healing during the early medieval period?

options.A: Monasteries and convents
options.B: Private community pharmacies
options.C: University teaching clinics
options.D: Government public health offices

explanation: Religious institutions like monasteries and convents housed the earliest organized healthcare and nursing services. [learn more](GNS112_U1_T2#GNS112_U1_T2_h2)

question: What is the very first thing you should do if a patient's tracheostomy tube accidentally pops out shortly after surgery?

options.A: Call the surgeon and wait at the bedside
options.B: Cover the open wound with sterile gauze permanently
options.C: Administer oral cough syrup to calm the patient
options.D: Attempt reinsertion using the bedside obturator

explanation: Don't panic! A fresh stoma can close up in minutes, blocking the airway. Grab that bedside obturator and try to pop the tube back in right away.

question: Why is keeping a close eye on a sedated patient such an important nursing duty?

options.A: The effect of sedatives exists on a sliding scale from calm to dangerous coma
options.B: Patients develop permanent neurological damage after a single dose
options.C: Medication clearance happens instantly through the skin
options.D: Sedatives consistently increase blood pressure and heart rate over time

explanation: Patients can drift easily from peaceful sleep into dangerously slow breathing. That is why watching them closely is a vital part of keeping them safe! [learn more](GNS223_U6_T2#GNS223_U6_T2_h1)

question: A nurse uses a bedside scanner to check a patient's wristband and a medication package before giving a pill. What safety feature is being used?

options.A: Barcode medication administration
options.B: Computerized provider order entry
options.C: Health information exchange network
options.D: Clinical decision support alerts

explanation: Scanning patient wristbands and medication packages prevents administration errors by verifying the right patient, drug, and dose. [learn more](GNS113_U2_T1#GNS113_U2_T1_h4)

question: Which type of transport needs cellular energy (ATP) to move nutrients against a concentration gradient?

options.A: Simple diffusion
options.B: Osmosis
options.C: Facilitated diffusion
options.D: Active transport

explanation: Spot on! When the body needs to push substances 'uphill' against a gradient, it has to spend energy (ATP)—hence the name active transport.

question: A mum receiving magnesium sulfate has a breathing rate of 8 breaths per minute and her knee reflexes are gone. What is your very first action?

options.A: Write it down as normal and keep watching.
options.B: Turn up the drip because the dose is too small.
options.C: Tell her to drink plenty of water.
options.D: Stop the magnesium infusion right away and tell the doctor.

explanation: Slow breathing and missing reflexes mean too much magnesium is building up in her body (toxicity)! Stop the infusion immediately and get help—calcium gluconate is the antidote.

question: Why are raw, crunchy vegetables excluded from a soft diet?

options.A: They contain too many vitamins that upset the stomach
options.B: They are too expensive for hospital meal planning
options.C: They change color too quickly on the food tray
options.D: They require too much chewing effort and can irritate the mouth

explanation: Raw vegetables are tough and fibrous, making them difficult to break down safely for someone on a soft diet. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T002#GNS227_U6_T002_h5)

question: Why could it backfire if you only consult wealthy community elites when planning a health project?

options.A: Elites are immune to most common infectious and tropical diseases
options.B: The elites may not represent or understand the actual needs of marginalized groups
options.C: Traditional leaders always forbid modern nursing practices in public spaces
options.D: The local government will fine the clinic for bypassing traditional protocols

explanation: It's easy to miss the struggles of the everyday person if you only talk to the wealthy leaders. Great nurses make sure to listen to voices from every corner of the community!

question: What is the golden rule of fluid balance when it comes to sodium?

options.A: Sodium ignores fluid shifts
options.B: Water follows sodium
options.C: Sodium follows protein
options.D: Water pushes sodium out

explanation: You got it! Think of sodium as a magnet—wherever sodium goes, water is definitely going to follow it.

question: A student nurse uses old patient charts from the archive to study infection rates from last year. What kind of data is this?

options.A: Primary data
options.B: Experimental data
options.C: Secondary data
options.D: Hypothetical data

explanation: Well done! Because the student is using pre-existing records gathered by someone else in the past, it's called secondary data.

question: Why do safety experts encourage a blame-free reporting culture in hospitals?

options.A: It encourages staff to report errors so systems can be fixed
options.B: It allows managers to punish careless workers more easily
options.C: It prevents nurses from ever making mistakes again
options.D: It stops patients from filing lawsuits against the hospital

explanation: Spot on! When nurses aren't afraid of being punished, they speak up about close calls. That honesty helps the whole team fix dangerous workflows.

question: How is gender expression different from gender identity?

options.A: Expression is the outward display of gender, while identity is the internal feeling
options.B: Expression has no connection to societal rules, unlike identity
options.C: Expression is fixed at birth, while identity changes daily
options.D: Expression refers only to chromosomes, while identity refers to hormones

explanation: Exactly right! Gender expression is what others can see (like clothing and behavior), whereas gender identity is a private, internal experience.

question: What is the main reason we use the coefficient of variation in research?

options.A: Calculating the exact sample size needed for a nursing study
options.B: Comparing variability between data sets with different units or means
options.C: Finding the absolute middle value of a skewed distribution
options.D: Eliminating all extreme outliers from a clinical data set

explanation: When comparing things measured in totally different ways (like age in years vs. weight in kg), the coefficient of variation helps us put them on a fair playing field.

question: How do researchers ethically manage control groups when testing a new treatment?

options.A: By making sure the control group pays for their own hospital stay
options.B: By hiding the true purpose of the study from the hospital staff
options.C: By refusing to give any care at all to the control group
options.D: By giving the control group standard nursing care instead of nothing

explanation: Providing standard care ensures patients in the control group are not neglected or harmed while still allowing comparison against the new intervention. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T7#GNS224_U1_T7_h7)

question: What makes water a polar molecule?

options.A: An unequal sharing of electrical charge between hydrogen and oxygen atoms
options.B: A complete absence of chemical bonds between its constituent atoms
options.C: An equal balance of heavy metal ions dissolved in its liquid state
options.D: The presence of long carbon chains running through its core

explanation: The oxygen atom pulls electrons closer to itself, giving water a slightly negative side and a slightly positive hydrogen side. Clever design!

question: What term is used to describe a dangerously low fasting blood sugar level?

options.A: Hypoglycemia
options.B: Hemoconcentration
options.C: Glycosuria
options.D: Hyperglycemia

explanation: Hypoglycemia refers to blood glucose levels falling below the normal healthy threshold, typically under 70 mg/dL. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T12#GNS221_U2_T12_h7)

question: What does the social ecology framework primarily examine when studying adolescent health?

options.A: The genetic history passed down from parents to the child
options.B: The entire surrounding environment and social network of the teenager
options.C: The specific biological changes happening during puberty
options.D: The financial status of the local healthcare facility

explanation: Social ecology looks at how multiple layers of a person's social environment interact to influence their overall health and behavior. [learn more](GNS312_U3_T20#GNS312_U3_T20_h1)

question: What normal, harmless feeling do many patients report right after the contrast dye goes in?

options.A: A sharp, shooting pain down both legs
options.B: An intense urge to vomit large amounts of fluid
options.C: Sudden numbness in the fingertips and toes
options.D: A temporary flushing feeling and metallic taste

explanation: Don't panic! Feeling a sudden warm flush and tasting metal in the mouth are totally normal, everyday reactions to the dye.

question: What does socioemotional selectivity theory say about older adults?

options.A: They experience a complete shutdown of all emotional responses
options.B: They tend to prioritize emotionally meaningful relationships and experiences
options.C: They seek out brand new friendships rather than maintaining old ones
options.D: They prefer to avoid all social contact and live completely isolated lives

explanation: As people get older, they prefer to invest their energy in deep, meaningful connections that bring true joy. Makes total sense!

question: What is the most important infection control practice for nurses doing perineal care or dressing changes?

options.A: Using scented antiseptic soaps for all skin surfaces
options.B: Wearing sterile gowns for routine temperature checks
options.C: Isolating the mother from her newborn baby
options.D: Rigorous hand hygiene and aseptic technique

explanation: Simple hand hygiene and clean sterile technique are your absolute best defenses against bringing new germs into healing wounds.

question: What is a common traditional barrier to assertiveness in hospitals?

options.A: Excessive training on communication skills
options.B: A complete lack of clinical handovers
options.C: Too many patient safety checklists
options.D: Strict medical hierarchy and fear of punishment

explanation: Traditional power structures often punish junior staff who question authority, creating fear around speaking up. [learn more](GST321_U7_T5#GST321_U7_T5_h4)

question: Why is a community diagnosis considered an ongoing cycle rather than a single event?

options.A: Because government funding stops after the first month
options.B: Because health needs change and progress must be evaluated
options.C: Because nurses are required to rewrite reports every week
options.D: Because community members refuse to answer questions twice

explanation: Communities change over time, and nurses must continuously evaluate whether interventions are working and what new problems have arisen. [learn more](GNS124_U3_T3#GNS124_U3_T3_h6)
